utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's all right now. Before I continue, I wish to tender this extract from the appropriate article of the criminal law of Yugoslavia which the witness mentioned as the basis for his conviction. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We'll take the next exhibit number, if we may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next exhibit number is D126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume we're in open session now, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 104, please tell me, in connection with the events you describe in the area of Bajina Basta, can you tell me when exactly you were in Bajina Basta, in what precise period of time, from when to when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there in different periods of time. This was in 1993 and 1994. But I have a poor memory for dates, so if I make a mistake, please make allowances for me. A lot of time has elapsed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when in 1993 were you there? If you have a poor memory not just for dates but for years, I don't understand how you can testify about events. When were you there? You say you were there in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given you the answer. He says 1993 and 1994, so we can't take the matter any further than that. If you want to ask him when in 1993, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'm asking him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you there in 1993 and when in 1994? Do you have any idea of the period of time you were active there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the spring and summer, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Spring and summer of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. As I said, I can't remember the exact years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And until when were you there in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to repeat that I was there at different intervals of time. I would spend 15 days there and then go away and come back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It seems to be difficult to establish this, but can you then explain, when was the last time you were there in 1994? Do you remember that, at least?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember that either? Very well. Well, were you there in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You weren't. Very well. As you weren't there in 1995, how is it possible that on page 8 in paragraph 9 you say that Franko Simatovic left Bajina Basta when the area was ethically cleansed in late 1995? You weren't there after 1994 and yet you claim that he was there until the end of 1995 when the area was ethnically cleansed. Where did you get this statement, then? Did you make this up just as you made up everything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment. That's a comment, Mr. Milosevic. Ask the question in proper form.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is a proper form, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It ended with a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, where did you get this, then? You weren't there in 1995, and you say he was there until the end of 1995 and that he left the area when it was ethnically cleansed. Where did you get this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I heard that from people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You heard that from hearsay, from people who were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is ridiculous, but I'll continue my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. That's a comment. You can make it in due course, but at the moment you're simply asking questions. You're wasting time with comments of that sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Bajina Basta is in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bajina Basta is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what sort of ethnic cleansing are you talking about? Because you say he left Bajina Basta when the area was ethnically cleansed. Who was it cleansed of ethnically? Of whom was Bajina Basta and that area cleansed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that the units were only stationed in Bajina Basta but their activities were carried out over the River Drina and their operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday to my direct question as to whether you participated and whether you had any kind of combat activity, you said all you did was reconnaissance flights and some sort of transport flights and medevacs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I did, but other units had other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the assignments of other units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific, but I know in general that they were in the area of the River Drina and that's where they carried out their combat operations. They crossed the River Drina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's clarify one point. It's put to you that you're wrong about something, but let us clarify it. When you were referring to an area being ethnically cleansed in 1995, which area were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the area across the River Drina, the area of Skelani, Osmace, that part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You only said you heard some rumours about this. Very well. Tell me, as you said that you yourself did not take part in combat operations, I will ask you about what you wrote on page 8 of your statement, something contained on page 8 of your statement. I will not mention names so we don't have to go into closed session, but please pay attention. You have the statement before you, page 8, paragraphs 3, 4, and 5. You say that Frenki arrived from Belgrade and that he called some names I won't mention. These were colleagues of yours, pilots, and you yourself. That's what you say. You say you were present, and that he told you he had met me, although he never met me, and that I ordered him that four Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. villages should be destroyed in the area of Srebrenica in the following four nights. That's what it says in your statement. You say you don't know the names of the villages and so on, and then you go on to explain how events proceeded after that. Tell me, did somebody destroy those villages, and is your statement correct in this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards this task --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear very well, although I've put these earphones on. The sound is very poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as regards this task, Mr. Frenki did come back from Belgrade and he asked us what could be done with a helicopter, what a helicopter could carry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Answer me first, did he tell you that he visited me? Did you mention me in this conversation, in your interview with the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't remember this. Well, and what about this task? Can you explain what happened? What assignment did he give you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't give me any assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say he invited four of you; you were the fourth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked us to see him because he wanted to know what a helicopter could carry and what could be done from a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he asked you what a helicopter could carry, but please, you say in the very next paragraph that you were told that they threw down four barrels full of liquid chemicals, poisons. "Frenki told them that the contents of a single barrel would kill all the people in an area the size of a football field." That's what it says in your statement. Do you know whether in the civil war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia any side used chemical weapons, poisons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they threw barrels of poisons on villages to destroy entire villages. That's what you say in your statement. Is this what you said, the way it's written here in the statement, or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, you haven't answered. Did you tell the investigators that they threw barrels with chemicals, this whole science fictional account about destroying villages with chemicals? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: That's what I heard they had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that poisons were used, either from a helicopter or on the ground or in any other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Did you hear -- the question is: Did you hear that poisons or a toxin or a chemical had been used? Which is what it says in your statement. Is that what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was this, tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the date now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you can't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you tell us from whom you did hear that? You can say it in private session, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I want to be in private session when I say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we then say that what is stated here in your statement is not correct? Because you say that he called and then he names certain people, including yourself, then he issued this assignment regarding four villages, and now you're saying that he wasn't present when he gave that assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have spent enough time on this. The witness has given his evidence, and we've heard you cross-examine. Let's move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on. There are quite a number of other questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. 104?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in answer to a question from Mr. Kwon, who noted that Jadar was a river, you said that it was a hill. And as a pilot, you are well versed with maps. Jadar is a river, Mr. 104. Do you know that? And Zeleni Jadar is a village, not a hill. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that it was Jadar. I said -- I was talking about Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But Zeleni Jadar is a village, not a hill. And what happened in Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Zeleni Jadar. Now, explain to me what happened in connection with Zeleni Jadar. Did you have an operation there or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered yesterday that I didn't have any operation at Zeleni Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Jadar. Now I wish to answer your other question that you put to me. At Zeleni Jadar there were operations conducted by the 63rd Parachute Brigade and the Vukovi from Drina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that when you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about it because the gentleman who was working with me was there. He was in Osmace at Zeleni Jadar. And the other gentlemen who were there told me about those combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then we would have to ask those gentlemen that you mentioned rather than you. Very well. Do you know what Frenki was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was the head of the unit that was stationed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was the head of the Intelligence Department of the security service and that he collected intelligence information? Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I see. But in your statement you say he was in command of the 63rd Parachute Brigade, the 74th Guards Brigade, et cetera. So explain, please, was that an error that you made or are you still claiming that he was in command of those military units even though he was not an officer of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To clarify what you asked me, Mr. Frenki was not in command of the 63rd Parachute Brigade, nor of the Guards Brigade. I said that there was a commander of the Parachute Brigade who was with me at the time; however, Mr. Frenki was in charge of all those operations around Bajina Basta. That was my impression, the impression I gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Groome asked you yesterday whether he issued orders, and you said that you personally had not noticed him giving orders to anyone. And then he asked you whether he was saluted to as a superior officer, and he [as interpreted] said you didn't see anyone saluting him as a superior officer. Is that right? That's what you said yesterday. Well, then explain, please, how did you get the idea that the head of the Intelligence Department of the security service could be in command of some military units. Where did that idea come from in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat. My unit, my part of the unit that was in the area had a superior officer who cooperated with Mr. Frenki and who agreed on any operations that were carried out in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. That was his evidence yesterday, Mr. Milosevic. It's not true that he never said that he was saluted. He did say that. The point he made, what he said was he never saw Frenki giving orders to members of the JNA or being saluted by them, but he was superior to the police units and the Wolves and was saluted by them. He was in charge of everything going on in Bajina Basta but there was always a VJ officer in charge of communications with him. So that distinction he did make yesterday. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were you present when these orders you mention were issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you present when any orders were issued to a JNA officer or when there were agreements being reached with a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I think I was, but I can't remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you can't remember. Very well. You say on page 6, paragraph 8, that Frenki and Arkan established the unit the Drina Wolves and that they established it in Knin under the name of Knindze. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was said to me by Mr. Max, Mr. Nedjo, and the other gentlemen who were in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me what you yourself know personally in your testimony. You probably know because you say that you know where they're from. These Drina Wolves were people from Bosnia; is that correct? Was this a police unit of the Republika Srpska? Is that something that is not sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please put me one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This unit that you call the Drina Wolves, was it a police unit of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whose unit was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unit, the Drina Wolves, were composed of the police of the Republic of Serbia and local villages from the area of Bajina Basta and Skelani and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And these villages, were they from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These villages were from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then explain to me, how could this unit have been established in Knin under the name of Knindze? Because that's what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this unit which was established in Knin was called Knindze. Part of that unit arrived and established the Drina Wolves in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, so this means that they arrived from the Krajina, the Knindze did, to Bajina Basta, and then they established the Drina Wolves. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that certain individuals arrived who were the basis of that unit, who were from the unit called Knindze, and they established the Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these people were in Knin? How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered that. He said he was told that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, all right. All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And time is almost up, Mr. Milosevic. You've got another two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two minutes is not enough for me, Mr. May. This nonsense has to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you said that the army had green camouflage uniforms, the police blue camouflage uniforms, and the Drina Wolves black uniforms; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army had green camouflage uniforms, and the police and the Drina Wolves wore blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of the Drina Wolves also wore black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the Drina Wolves also wore green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they wore green and blue and black uniforms, these Drina Wolves, but you cannot remember how many of them there were. I asked you yesterday how many of these Drina Wolves there were whom you saw there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these Drina Wolves, their number, I don't know that because most of the members of the unit were engaged in combat operations across the River Drina. It was only the corps of the unit and the logistical support that was located in the hotel in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the people you describe whose uniforms you saw, you say they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were not on the other bank of the Drina. You saw them in Bajina Basta. How many of them did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these people who made up the corps of the unit in Bajina Basta, and I also saw them in white jeeps, Defender-type jeeps, owned by the police of the Republic of Serbia. I saw them crossing the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how many of them were there, the ones you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said yesterday that there were about 100 of these men whom I saw, but I don't know the exact number because I never counted them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this must be your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is absolutely insufficient. This cannot be allowed because this witness has said all sorts of things and his statement is very long. I don't know how you think I can -- I can cross-examine him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His statement, in fact, is I think eight or nine pages. So compared with many of the statements we have in this case, it's not long. You were told the time that you have, and you must tailor your cross-examine accordingly. But you can ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in your statement I did not see you say that there were any convicts in this unit. Yesterday Mr. Groome asked you whether there were convicts in the unit and you said there was a man nicknamed Pacov, is that correct, Pacov meaning "rat"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, when asked, I responded that the lady who was Mr. Frenki's secretary had told me that Mr. Pacov was a former convict from a prison in Kosovo and that Mr. Frenki took him out of prison and brought him to that battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Frenki's secretary told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did she tell you anything else? Were there any other convicts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you feel that as a soldier or a former soldier that this fact was important, that there was a convict in a unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you think it's important, why is it not in the statement that you made when you were interviewed by the investigators? Why did you withhold this important fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I probably forgot to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did you manage to remember it yesterday, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first of all, I should like to ask you something about the things that you told us yesterday in the examination-in-chief answering questions from the Prosecution. You said yesterday that on one occasion you saw in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina in certain locations a large number of victims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't say yesterday that on one occasion you saw victims as you were flying in your helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention victims at all yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours in what connection you mentioned those victims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that a colleague who was with me had told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you personally didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you said yesterday that on two occasions you took part in deliveries of certain material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't say that when you were interviewed by the investigator of the Prosecution. In your first statement you did not mention at all your participation in any such activities. Can you explain that to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you did not belong to a unit that was under the command of Frenki.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in your statement which you gave to the investigators -- I don't know whether you have it in front of you over there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 5, paragraph 6 of the English version. And I'll read what it says in the B/C/S version. You said that going to Bajina Basta, you were assigned to a unit under Frenki's command. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that I was assigned to a unit of which Mr. Frenki was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were in a unit under another commander a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I explained how the command structure functioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Here in your statement, page 5, paragraph 5 of the English version, it says that you arrived in Bajina Basta and Skelani in the winter of 1993. A moment ago you mentioned the spring and the summer. Which is true; what you said here or in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was there for the first time in Bajina Basta and Skelani, that was between the winter and the spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. But what you said at the time, you said that the very first time that you were in Bajina Basta you stayed at a hotel in Bajina Basta; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent only one night in that hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But where did you stay otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the elementary school in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how many times did you take Frenki in your helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Not even approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you took him to Belgrade, as you said yesterday, where were you sitting when you were driving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why in the back, when you're an operator, navigator, and a pilot? Who was sitting in your place as the operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't this dangerous for the flight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me something else: You said on a number of occasions that you had heard from other people in Frenki's unit what was being planned and what was being done, but in your statement you said that they never mentioned what assignments would be carried out by men in his unit. Is that right? This is page 8, paragraph 1 of the English version. Is that true, that they never spoke about the actions they were undertaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They and his men never spoke about operations or activities that they were undertaking, but from stories, from conversations when they returned from those operations, one could learn of various details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-104, in response to a question that Mr. Tapuskovic just put to you, you said that on most occasions when you were in Bajina Basta you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stayed at an elementary school in Skelani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the first time I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The time that you stayed in the elementary school in Skelani, were you directed to that school by somebody at -- in Bajina Basta who was in a position of responsibility or was that your own decision to go and stay at that elementary school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told to go to that elementary school by Mr. Maksi [phoen]. He gave instructions to me and my associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Skelani is in what republic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skelani is in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. B-104, to clarify this matter, I'd like to ask this question once again. I'll read out some passages in your statement. It is on page 7, around the sixth paragraph. "I remember an occasion but not date or even year when Frenki came back from Belgrade. He called ..." Some colleagues of yours; I will not name it here, "... and me, telling us that he met with the president (Milosevic) who had ordered the destruction of four villages in the Srebrenica area within the next four nights." To the question put to you by the accused, you said that you don't remember this. Could you clarify this. Is this also what you heard from your colleagues, or you don't remember this at all? How come this passage could appear in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Frenki, when he returned from Belgrade, invited us to an informal meeting and asked us about ways in which it was possible to act from a helicopter, as I have explained. However, who Mr. Frenki met with in Belgrade, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-104, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for making yourself available to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next witness is outside. And there's also Mr. McKeon here, if the Court would wish to deal with the 92 bis matter now; whichever the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go on with the evidence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a protected witness, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need protective measures. Well, we've made the order, have we, in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was an order. I can get the date, if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's merely a question of getting -- before we forget, the accused produced an exhibit, and I don't know if we have it or not. Did we have -- did we have the exhibit from the accused? If so, perhaps it could be collected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think better, if we can, to hear the evidence. We'll find a moment towards the end of the day to deal with the legal argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls B-1493.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The order has been made, so we're not going to go back on that. We will see what the position is when he gives his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in an exercise of caution, could I ask the registrar to check whether that last bit of colloquy was done in open court. It appears in the transcript that the discussion about the witness's position may have been done in public court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it was in open session. So I will redact it, if requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown tab 1 of the -- an exhibit binder. And if possible, I ask that it be assigned a number at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness B-1493, I'd ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 425, tab 1. Is that your name and date of birth at the top of that sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I have looked at the document, and all the information it contains is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is your name contained on that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes. I signed this document on the 24th of March, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does that document also contain a summary of your educational and professional background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The document does contain all the information regarding my educational background and working experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that document. I'd ask that we briefly go into private session for a few background questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this can be a reason for the witness to testify in secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He is not examined secretly. As you know quite well, much of it is in open session. Some of it is in private session. That is not in secret. It's in private session. There's a distinction. Now, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I just ask that that last question be redacted, as it reveals his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, we are now in open session. My first question to you is: In March of 1991 as a high-ranking member of the JNA, did you become aware of the formulation of an emergency plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes. In March of 1991, my command, in which I had a very senior position for operative and wartime planning, received an order to prepare a plan for the use of units in the case of an emergency. When I examined that plan, up until then and from 1988 I had compiled a number of plans, but it seemed rather strange to me because this was the first time for us to be doing something like that. I personally was involved on a part of that plan, that is, the preparation of maps, ethnic maps for the territory in Croatia. We had to indicate clearly and highlight even the smallest village in the colour corresponding to ethnicity and indicate the exact number of inhabitants, Croats, Serbs, and others. Also, we had to mark every important bridge, radio relay transmitter, communication centres, and both civilian and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you said that this plan was different than other plans you had worked on in the past. How was it different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: It was different because up until then we hadn't prepared any plans based on ethnicity, but we were devising plans that would involve all the inhabitants of Yugoslavia without any consideration given to ethnic composition. Secondly, the plan mentioned the possible -- a possible internal enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did it specify who this internal enemy was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes. The plan mentioned the potential internal enemies could be extremist parts of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this plan, did this plan have an imagined scenario that was used to develop particular points about the plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: As I said, I worked on only a part of that plan, that is, the map. The first document of the plan consisted of the order for the use of JNA units and units of the Territorial Defence. And each unit would be attributed an area of responsibility within that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you complete your work on this plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And from -- from whom did you receive the directive to work on this plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: It was called an excerpt or an abstract for the preparation of a plan. My unit received it from the command of the 1st Military District in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've talked about March 1991 as the time that you were asked to do this plan. Was the plan completed around that same time period or did it take longer than March?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Towards the end of the plan, there was a deadline indicating when the plan had to be completed and a copy of the plan had to be forwarded to the command of the 1st Military District in Belgrade, and the deadline was April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to events in Croatia in May of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, I need to clarify something. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention to events in Croatia in May of 1991. I would point out to the Chamber that the locations that he will refer to can be found on mapbook -- Prosecution Exhibit 336, page 23, and it would be the intersection of D2. Sir, in May of 1991, were you involved in a joint detachment that was sent to the Borovo Selo area of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In May -- to be more precise, on the 2nd of May, 1991, after the events in Borovo Selo, I was called by my commander and given orders to be the commander of a joint detachment which needed to go and station itself in Vinkovci, where it would be given more specific assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber what were the individual units Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that made up this joint detachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: It's called a joint detachment because it is not a unit that is a part of the establishment but is composed of several diverse units so that it consisted of one platoon of APCs, one platoon of Pragas - or air defence - one platoon of military police, one platoon of scouts, one platoon of engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you use the word "Praga," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Praga is a combat armoured vehicle of Czech manufacture intended for targeting in the air, and it is very effective for use with the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the time you left for this mission, what was your understanding of the task that was being given to this joint detachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: When I went on that mission, I knew roughly because I had been informed that a similar such detachment had been formed in Slavonia and that it was already on its way along the route Osijek-Nustar-Borovo Selo and that our assignment was to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did your part of this detachment arrive in Vinkovci at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: We arrived, as planned, around 9.00 or 9.30 in the evening in Vinkovci. We stationed ourselves in the barracks in Vinkovci. I told the troops to take a rest and I also rested in the night between the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the first night that you were in Vinkovci, could you hear anything in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Throughout the night shooting could be heard, firing mainly from infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could you tell the direction from which that fire came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes. One could tell that it was coming from the direction of the villages of Mirkovci and Jankovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, those villages, can you tell the Chamber what is the ethnic make-up of those two respective villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The village of Mirkovci is about 7 and a half or 8 kilometres from Vinkovci. The village of Jankovci about 10, 10 and a half kilometres from Vinkovci. Mirkovci is 100 percent Serb populated. The village of Jankovci is about 95 per cent Croat populated. There are six households that were occupied by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so it's clear, it appears that on the map there are two locations with the name of Jankovci in it. Is there another name or a more precise definition of Jankovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: There's a road going from Vinkovci to the village of Mirkovci, and then as you go on you will come across the village of Jankovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that page 23 of the mapbook be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you just to take the pointer in front of you and indicate Jankovci that you're referring to in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. There we note two Jankovcis, one Stari Jankovci and another Novi Jankovci. Could you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're moving from Vinkovci, the village of Mirkovci, and then the village of Old Jankovci, Stari Jankovci, where it says "Stari Jankovci." But Stari and Novi Jankovci are virtually linked together and now they are one village. And it was in the area of Stari Jankovci, at this crossroads here, in the direction of Mirkovci, right next to the road there are three Serb households. One house is across the way from the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention now to the first full day that you were in Vinkovci. Can you please describe what, if anything, you and this joint detachment did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In the morning, when we got up, we had breakfast as usual and engaged in preparations. And about 11.00 I was called up by radio link, and I received on the printer an order from my commander for the use or deployment of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how were you to deploy the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Let me add that that morning, too, the shooting could be heard, and the order said that I had to organise a column in combat formation to head along the indicated route to investigate what was happening between the villages of Mirkovci and Jankovci and possibly to link up with the next joint detachment, which had been dispatched from Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you in fact do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: At a quarter past 11.00, roughly, I set off with a column. I reached the first houses prior to the village of Mirkovci, and on the road I came across a roadblock, a barricade. That was the first time I saw any such thing since I have been an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say "roadblock," can you describe in a little greater detail what it was that was blocking the road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: On that road there were four iron hedgehogs. To the left and the right there were sandbags piled up. And behind this protective pile was a machine-gun pointed towards Vinkovci. In the middle of that obstacle was a soldier. He was wearing a uniform. That's why I called him a soldier. But when I saw him, I was astonished, flabbergasted. He was wearing complete Chetnik uniforms; he had a firm hat on his head, bandoliers across his chest, he was holding a machine-gun in his hands, he had special kind of trousers. He stopped the column. He stood in front of us and stopped us and said that we couldn't pass until we were given approval by his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you've used the word "hedgehog." Am I correct in thinking that what you were referring to is a set of iron girders bolted together in such a way as to make it impossible for a vehicle to drive over them or around them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you're indicating an X-shape with your fingers to indicate what the appearance of a hedgehog looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Hedgehogs are mostly made from old iron girders, and they consist of three such girders and are usually used to block roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The person that you've described being in this Chetnik uniform, did you have a conversation with this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: No. He just said to me, because I was at the head of the column, "You can't pass until you're given permission by my commander." And I asked him, "And who is your commander?" And he said, "He's in that house." It was about 20 metres away. And I said, "Can you call that command of yours?" And then he actually did go off, and in about ten minutes a man came out dressed in the same manner as he, and he came up to me and asked me, "Who are you?" And I told him that we were a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army whose assignment was to establish order in the area, and I said, "Please remove these hedgehogs so we can pass." He answered, "To remove the hedgehogs, I have to receive permission from my commander." Then I asked him, "And who is your commander?" And he said, "My command is in Sremska Mitrovica, so please allow me to go and telephone, to ask for permission or not, and then I'll let you know." And indeed he went off, returned very quickly, and said, "I have been given permission from Sremska Mitrovica," and this soldier who was there before him removed two hedgehogs and we went on through the village of Mirkovci towards the village of Jankovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask my next question, what time would the Chamber want to break this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Witness B-1493, we are going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. During this adjournment and any others there may be in the case while you're giving your evidence, don't speak to anybody, please, about it until it's over and don't let anybody speak to you about it, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes. If you'll be back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, before we continue, I want to ask a few more questions about this roadblock. Is it true that altogether there were three men manning this roadblock?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: That's correct. There were two men manning the machine-guns and one man standing in the middle of the barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That three men, does that include the person or the commander who was up in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've described the uniform that one of them was wearing. How were the other men at this roadblock dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: All four of them, in fact, including the commander, were wearing the same uniforms with the same insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said that the first person you talked -- or, I'm sorry, the commander of the roadblock, when you spoke to him, he said that he had to check with his commander in Sremska Mitrovica. In what republic is Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Sremska Mitrovica is in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did any of the men at the roadblock identify the name of the unit or organisation that they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Neither the commander who came nor the soldiers manning the barricade revealed to me what unit was stationed in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many men did you have in the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: There were about 120 men in total in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why it was you followed this procedure of allowing him to get permission rather than simply forcibly going through the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: First of all, I was surprised when I saw that on the road, men wearing such uniforms, although I had heard before that that such things were happening. But this was the first time I had experienced personally a barricade and people in those uniforms, and the main reason I didn't use force to go through the barricade was that this was not my task. My task was quite the opposite. My commander had told me to restore order and to make sure that there was no shooting, no firing in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long were you held at the barricade before they allowed you to pass through it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: This all lasted about 25 minutes or half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did you go when you passed through the barricade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: When I passed through the barricade, I passed through the village of Mirkovci, and then there is a small bend. And when I arrived at the bend, I saw that at the end of the village of Jankovci there was a house on fire and that there was shooting there, so I went with the column in the direction of the village of Jankovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Mirkovci. As you passed through that village, did you notice anything unusual, such as evidence of fighting or houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In the village of Mirkovci, there was nothing very unusual. You could hear shooting coming from the direction of Jankovci. But in the village itself there was nothing going on. But I didn't see anyone in the street. There was almost nobody around, or around the houses next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you do when you arrived in Jankovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Before I arrived in Jankovci, when I saw that there was a house on fire about half a kilometre or a little more away, I stopped the column, I deployed the APCs in battle order, I called the military police and sent him off with a Praga to see what the shooting was about, why the house was on fire, simply to reconnoitre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your time in Jankovci, were you able to speak with one of the community leaders of that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: When my military police patrol came back, they reported that there was a group of armed men who fled in the direction of the village of Mirkovci when the patrol arrived. I redeployed the joint detachment in a house in between the two villages, and I sent couriers and my assistant to look for the presidents of the local communes of Mirkovci and Jankovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The military police that reported back to you, did they describe what, if any, uniforms these armed men were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes. They said they had seen those four men. One had even dropped a walkie-talkie which was handed over to my command, and they said they were wearing the same sort of uniforms as the men we had seen at the barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The walkie-talkie that was handed over to you, did you recognise this as a piece of equipment from the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: At that time the Yugoslav People's Army did not use such means of radio communication. The smallest radio station was RUP 3. And that was used at squad and company level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you convened a meeting between the local municipality presidents of both Mirkovci, the Serb village, and Stari Jankovci, the Croat village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: First the representative of the MUP from Vinkovci arrived. About ten minutes later, the president of the local commune of Jankovci arrived, and about half an hour later - and it was already evening, about 6.30 - the president of the local commune of Mirkovci arrived. Then we started a meeting of all of us in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to summarise briefly what was told to you at -- during the course of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I have to point out, I said that in the village of Jankovci the first three houses before the crossroads and one after the crossroads were Serbian houses. The people from that house came and they asked that the army remain there to protect them and the village. They said that some people had been infiltrated, that they were not even from Mirkovci. And as I said, the joint detachment had been sent there to protect the people. With the presidents of the local communes and the representative of the MUP from Vinkovci, I explained to them first of all what my task was, the task I had been given by my superior officer, and I said that all operations had to be stopped; otherwise, I would have to use force in order to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the people at this meeting identify or describe these infiltrators that they told you about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: It was the president of the local commune of Mirkovci who said that the men who had set up the barricade in Mirkovci and who had done what they had done in the village of Jankovci, that these were not local people from the village of Mirkovci, that they were people who had been infiltrated from outside. Then they told me that between the two villages there had been no conflicts for centuries, that co-existence was exceptionally good, that they always exchanged visits at Christmas and Easter, that there were many marriages between the villages -- between the inhabitants of the two villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that the record is clear, is it your testimony that you were informed that the infiltrators were the people who damaged these three houses in Jankovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I was told that these were people who had been infiltrated. The president of Mirkovci told me this. And they damaged a Croatian house which was next to the first Serbian house behind the crossroads. There was an inn on the ground floor and there were two floors above where people resided, and that was the only house that was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the evening of the 3rd of May, did you send a report to your superiors regarding your observations of the situation in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: On completion of every combat task in the JNA, the commander was duty-bound before 2200 hours to send a regular daily combat report. And after the meeting I have described, that's what I did. I sent a report to my command directly where I described how I had set out, what I had found, and what I had done. I also told them how I had deployed my units, what kind of obstacles I had come across, what people. And this was received by the head of the operations centre in my command who forwarded it immediately to the command of the 1st Military District in Belgrade. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you in this report recount the events at the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I described everything, everything that I have just said in my testimony. All this was in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that the military police, your military police, informed you that this group of infiltrators had fled in the direction of Mirkovci. After that point in time, was there any other shooting or conflict in that area for the time that you remained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: During the night, between the 3rd and the 4th of May, 1991, for the most part there was not much shooting. You could hear sporadic shooting at the end of the village of Mirkovci, but you couldn't describe it as firing on the village of Jankovci. It was probably to intimidate people or shooting by drunken men, but the situation was quite calm, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you deploy the men under your command in such a way as to attempt to separate and to prevent further conflicts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: As I said, when I brought the column to the area between Mirkovci and Jankovci, I did that right away because, when I arrived, that's when the conflicts were at their highest point and that's when I deployed my unit. When the military police patrol came back, we simply improved the deployment a little bit and we had to secure people. We had to provide for security during the night to avoid surprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you received a response to the report that you filed with your superiors on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: On the 4th, in the morning, I received a reply from my superior officer that I should remain and provide security with the same kind of deployment I had set up up to that point. On the 4th of May, in that area you could hear sporadic shooting here and there but there were no operations going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, at around 10.00, a colleague of mine arrived in a 101 vehicle with an order from my superior commander saying that he was now appointed commander of that joint detachment and that I was to return to my command. So we carried out a handover of duties and I was ordered to stop in the village of Sid, where I was to pick up two soldiers on their way from Belgrade. And that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this unusual for you to receive such an order in the middle of carrying out a mission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes. Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After you left this area, did you learn what happened with the joint detachment that was now stationed in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: After my departure, around the 7th of May, between the 7th and the 8th, there were intense conflicts in the area between the villages of Mirkovci and Jankovci and one might say that that's when war really broke out in that area. I can say that the heads of the households in those four houses sent a letter to my superior command on the 6th of May asking for me to be sent back to the area. This document is in existence in the operations centre of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to your command, did you have a conversation with your superior officer regarding the events in this -- in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: When I returned to my command, of course in the line of duty I went to see my commander who had appointed me to that post to give him an oral report. But as soon as I entered his office, he said to me, "What kind of report did you send?" And I said, "Well, it was a regular combat report." And he said, "What sort of Chetniks did you see? You saw tomcats."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was your response?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I said, "Commander, I saw real men, Chetniks, the kind I've seen in films, the films entitled "Kozara," "Sutjeska," and "Neretva." And he said, "That's impossible."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether or not he -- did he tell you about the response of the 1st Military District to your report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that. I heard that from the chief of the operations centre, that there had been a reaction in the 1st Military District. They criticised my superior officer because of the report that had been forwarded to them. They said he should have checked it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, around the same period of time, was the composition of the officers in your corps changing, the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: At that time, in my command, the superior -- I was the only non-Serb, along with another officer of Croatian ethnicity, who were in high-ranking positions. Otherwise, the head and -- or the chief and all his assistants were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Had it always been like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Always? No, it had not always been like that, from the time my unit was established. But after -- or rather, from 1988, when it was established, it was mixed. The corps command was mainly of that composition, but at brigade level there were non-Serb officers. However, in 1990, practically not a single commander from battalion level upwards was a non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Around this period of time, the summer and going into the fall of 1991, was your access to information that you previously had access to, was that restricted in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I told you in the beginning that in my superior command I had a very important role in operative and war planning. But after my return some 15 days later, I was ordered to hand over this duty, and I was denied access to the operations room where war planning was conducted. I continued carrying out duties in that department, but they were not duties connected with war planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Had you been cited for any misconduct or were there any pending accusations against you which could have explained this change in the access that you had to this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I was never disciplined, but it was a punishment for me that I was not allowed to continue doing the job I had done since 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Around the same period of time, were you witness to a speech made before a large group of JNA soldiers that caused you concern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Sometime in the autumn, I think it was October, I was part of a team that had the task of carrying out the mobilisation of a brigade in Bijeljina. I remember that Colonel Novica Simic had been designated a commander of that brigade, and after mobilisation the brigade was to march and take part in war operations in the area of Okucani and Gradiska. We had various tasks to do with mobilisation, and at the time I was one of the officers in charge of mobilisation. I had been completely removed from my previous duties and sidelined and sent to a completely different department. The mobilisation went on for two days, and one battalion of that brigade was mobilised from the area of Bijeljina and its surrounding area, while another battalion came from the area of Sabac and the surrounding villages, and the third one was from Sremska Mitrovica and the surrounding area. The battalions arriving from Serbia were wearing JNA uniforms, but 90 per cent of them were not wearing on their caps the insignia worn by the JNA. Instead, they had Chetnik insignia. There was no reaction to this. The leader of our team did not react. We carried out the mobilisation, we formed the brigade. And at about 1500 hours, the brigade was lined up. At this line-up the leader of my team received a report. He was at the rank of general. And he held a speech. We called this moral, political preparation of the brigade for carrying out their task. He did not greet the brigade with the greeting that had previously been used in the JNA. He did not say, "Comrade soldiers, I greet you" but he started with, "God help you brave men." Then he said, "You are brave Serbian heroes who are to set out from here to protect and defend the Serbian people in the Republic of Croatia." And he said other things to that effect, but this is what I remember. My colleagues and I, even those who were Serbs, were surprised by this speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just a few questions regarding this event. Can you tell us, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. how many men are ordinarily in a brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: That depends on the brigade. This was a light brigade, and it numbers about 1.500 to 2.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the speech that you're describing for us now was in front of 1.500 to 2.000 men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You described that the people that were mobilised from Serbia had different headgear on than was ordinarily worn by the JNA. Would that have been considered a violation of JNA regulations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The soldiers who were mobilised in the area of Sabac and Sremska Mitrovica, a large number of them did not wear the Titovka caps as were worn by JNA members. They were wearing Sajkaca, another type of cap, and on those caps they didn't have the five-cornered star but a Chetnik badge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would that have been in violation of JNA regulations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Under normal conditions, this could not have happened. But under those conditions, when already things were -- this was certainly a very, very serious violation of the rules and regulations in the Yugoslav People's Army at the time. And before that people would be held responsible and sent to prison for such an act.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the content of the speech that was made to these men, would that have been considered an appropriate way to address members of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: This was the first time that I heard anyone addressing a unit of the still-JNA in that way. Secondly, never until then had I heard anything like that being said to a unit that was being prepared for an assignment, even in peacetime. I had never heard a speech along those lines before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to now draw your attention to another subject. Did you become aware during the course of your official duties of members of the Territorial Defence from the Republic of Serbia being deployed outside of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: While performing my duties, I learnt and saw members of the Territorial Defence from the Republic of Serbia being used or deployed in territories outside the Republic of Serbia. A brigade of the Territorial Defence of Loznica on a number of occasions would come from Loznica to where I was located to rest there, to be replenished, spend the night, and from there it would go on to perform wartime assignments in the Republic of Croatia. Similarly, I know that a battalion of the Territorial Defence from the Republic of Serbia during the attack on Zvornik was used for that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, just so the record is clear, in what republic is Loznica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Loznica is in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber what is your understanding of what has to be done or who has to give approval before members of one republic's Territorial Defence can be deployed outside of that republic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in Yugoslavia was formed at the level of republics and there was a republican staff of the Territorial Defence which was subordinated to the political leadership, virtually to the president of the republic, and the republican staff was subordinated in all of Yugoslavia's republics to the presidents of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now to another topic. Were you aware during the course of your official duties that there was an effort to take the arms from the territorial depots in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: An order was issued by the general staff of the Army of Bosnia -- no, an order was issued by the general staff of the JNA that all the weapons of the Territorial Defence which used to be stored in the warehouses of the TO, it was secured there, cleaned, and used during military exercises, that it should be seized from the Territorial Defence and placed in warehouses under the control of the JNA. This was carried out 100 per cent in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, almost also in Croatia but they didn't manage to do that in Slovenia because the Slovenes did not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To your knowledge, in the area of which you have knowledge, was this done uniformly despite the different ethnic compositions of the respective municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The weapons of the Territorial Defence were seized and placed under the control and in the warehouses of the JNA uniformly regardless of ethnic affiliation, of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you later learn that some of these weapons were redistributed after they had been taken and placed in the control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, in February, March, weapons of the TO started to be issued and transported from JNA warehouses and started to be distributed mostly to municipal staffs of the Territorial Defence in municipalities inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you learn this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I personally saw the loading of weapons and columns driving the weapons away, columns of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you name some of the specific locations that you have personal knowledge were armed in this way?
