utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: From my location, weapons were taken to Vlasenica, Sekovici, Lopare, Ugljevik. That is what I saw, the columns leaving and the weapons being loaded. This was roughly around March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has already heard evidence regarding withdrawal of troops from Slovenia and Croatia. I want to ask you not to focus on the withdrawal itself, but can you comment on your observations regarding where the withdrawing troops, if they did, where they took up positions in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Mostly the units that were coming from the Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia would come to Bosnia-Herzegovina, where they were deployed. In the area where I was stationed, a very strong unit arrived, known as the 4th Armoured Brigade from Jastrebarsko, in Croatia, and it was deployed mostly in locations where the municipalities with a majority Serb population were located. I can say that this brigade consisted of a battalion of tanks, T-84 tanks, and two battalions had T-55. And they were deployed -- one battalion was in the area of Sekovici and the villages in Sekovici municipality; one battalion from Zvornik towards Bijeljina; and a third battalion secured the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many tanks would be in a battalion of tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: A battalion consists of 31 tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as best you can recall, what were -- what was the time period when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: This brigade arrived in the autumn of 1991, and I know that the brigade commander, together with the other commanders in that area of responsibility, was received by the president of that municipality, which was the largest municipality in that area, towards New Year's Eve.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the primary warehouses in your command were emptied and the goods therein transported to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Regarding the warehouses, the commands, and the units in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, attempts were made to avoid all the weaknesses and omissions made by the JNA in Slovenia and especially in Croatia. Namely, all warehouses and all units and commands that were in areas with mixed populations or majority Croatian or Bosniak populations, that those warehouses be moved from there and relocated to areas with majority Serb populations. The same applied to all headquarters or commands. They, too, were relocated to areas and towns with a majority Serb population. And by the end of March 1992, this process had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the officers in your command to these events, this transfer of troops and transfer of munitions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In those days, we non-Serb officers had already realised that something was in the offing in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. It became clear to us in the first place because not a single non-Serb officer went together with his high command to a new location, but usually non-Serb officers, and also Serb officers who were married to a Croat or a Bosniak, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would remain at the old location of the command and would perform subsidiary activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address the Chamber before I put this next exhibit to the witness? The witness very recently has provided a videotape to the Office of the Prosecutor. In fact, the copies for disclosure won't be available until 9.00 tomorrow morning. I just at this point seek to mark it for identification, ask the witness a couple of questions regarding its origin, and then when a transcript is available and when both sides have had an opportunity to view it, at that point possibly tender the exhibit. But simply marked for identification at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that this exhibit, which is tab 5 of Prosecution 425, be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I ask you: Yesterday, did you view a copy of a tape that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor recently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that the copy that you're holding in your hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How do you know that that's the copy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Because I reviewed it and I signed it on the 8th of April, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you just in a sentence or two summarise for the Chamber, what is this tape? What's contained on this tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: On this tape the commander of the 2nd Military District, General Colonel Kukanjac, in June 1992 is giving an interview to Risto Djogo, a journalist of the Serbian television station SRNA. What is important regarding this tape - and I shall put it briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I'm going to interrupt, if I may. I think we may need to consider the admissibility of this tape before we go any further. When we've got a transcript, we can look at it and decide whether it's admissible or not. I notice the type of evidence it is. There are sometimes objections. It may be in this case there won't be, but we ought to consider it before we go any further or hear any other evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I just ask him how he came into possession of the tape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how you came into possession of this tape.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: This tape was a recording from the Serbian television SRNA programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during the course of your duties, were you familiar with the voice -- did you have interaction with Lieutenant General -- or General Colonel Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I worked with General Kukanjac for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that his voice that's on the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: His voice, his image.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now draw your attention to the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina in March of 1992. Can you please tell us what your reaction and the reaction of some of the other soldiers in your command was to this referendum.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: First of all, in those days I didn't have any soldiers under my command because, as I had told you, I had been sidelined to a less significant position. I can say that most of the officers in my command, even some Serbs, voted at that referendum. And in view of the developments and the course of events in Yugoslavia, it was quite normal for such a referendum to be held in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina when all the other attempts, the attempt at confederation or nothing else was successful, Croatia and Slovenia had already been granted independence, so that we considered it normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've already heard evidence about this. I think we will deal with what the witness himself saw or heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now to the latter part of May 1992, after the JNA officially withdrew from Bosnia. Can you describe for us what, if any, personal knowledge you have regarding the involvement of the Yugoslav army in Bosnia after that date and time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: After the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the virtual cessation of its existence as the Yugoslav People's Army on the 4th or whether it was the 19th of May that it became the Army of Yugoslavia, I am familiar with the participation of units of the Army of Yugoslavia in activities in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the specific instances which you have knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: First of all, I can say that the involvement of the Novi Sad Corps occurred on several occasions in the area of the corridor, Posavina Corridor, especially in October 1992, when the Posavski corridor was being secured and broadened. And this fact was confirmed by an officer who, during the operation of the Novi Sad Corps, was captured together with three other soldiers and who was interrogated by our organs and he confirmed that he belonged to the Novi Sad Corps. And this same person several months later was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are there any other examples of which you have personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I know about this and I had personal contact with this major. I also am aware of the participation of the Uzice Corps in the region of Skelani, near Bratunac, and Srebrenica, also the involvement of the Uzice Corps in the region of Gorazde and in those places in -- along the Drina River Valley. And it is known for certain that those units were under the direct command of General Ojdanic, as he was the commander of the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask you to be as precise as possible in telling us when it was that the Uzice Corps was involved in these different areas.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The Uzice Corps in the area of Skelani and Gorazde participated from May 1992 up until about July 1992. That is the information I received from my intelligence organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the question of paramilitaries. Can you please describe what you know about the use of paramilitaries in some of the events in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, the event that I described in Mirkovci, the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina started with the infiltration and activities of these paramilitary units. The first such unit, very well organised unit, very well trained and very well organised, was infiltrated from the Republic of Serbia into Bosnia and Herzegovina in the region of Bijeljina, and we are aware of the event that occurred in Bijeljina so that I don't have to describe it. Also, the use of these paramilitary units - I would never call them paramilitary, I'd call them special, well-trained units - they were used throughout the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the very use of that unit in 1995, when the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was about to liberate Bijeljina, Arkan's brigade arrived, joined in, and virtually halted the further progress of the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at a most important point of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe, based upon your military experience, what function these special troops performed in the military plans or the military events as you became aware of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Again, I won't call them anything but special units. And their task was the same as during the aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina; at the beginning of the war, to infiltrate certain areas, shall we say Bijeljina Zvornik, to cause chaos there, to kill 30, 50, or several civilians, mostly men of some prestige. That was always done, that people of repute be liquidated in a particular town. To loot, to cause disruption and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. thereby lead to JNA units blocking the area and in fact taking part in the occupation of those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was the command that you were part of in the JNA aware of the presence of and the activities of these special units, as you call them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: As soon as the first unit arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the command, of which I was a member, knew about it, knew that the unit had arrived from the Republic of Serbia, and what it had done in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was your -- the position of your commander or the commander of your corps regarding these special units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The commander of the corps at the time, together with units of the Yugoslav People's Army, as it was still the Yugoslav People's Army, did not react or respond at all to the activities of this special unit. There was no reaction to the fact that from another state, which was by then another state, a unit had been infiltrated and had actually committed a crime against the civilian population, though this was the duty of the Yugoslav People's Army to do so because it said in black letters in our rules that in addition to the protection of the integrity of Yugoslavia, it was the task of the JNA to protect the security and safety of the population of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to Bijeljina. The Chamber has heard extensive evidence on what has happened in Bijeljina. I want you to describe for the Chamber to the extent you're able what resources of the JNA were present in Bijeljina or in the vicinity of Bijeljina at the time of the end of March, early April 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In Bijeljina itself, the division command was stationed. From Zvornik toward Sepak-Janja, most of the 2nd Battalion of the 4th Armoured Brigade were deployed. At the entrance to Bijeljina, from one direction -- in any event all the approaches to Bijeljina were blocked by units of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you assist us by putting in very simple terms the number -- or the size of the JNA presence there. Maybe simply by telling us the approximate number of men that would have been deployed and the different types of equipment that would have been deployed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In Bijeljina itself, there weren't many men in the barracks itself. There may have been 100 or a little over. I know that for certain. Less than 200. But around Bijeljina, there were deployed about 18 tanks and three infantry and one motorised battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what would comprise -- or what would a motorised battalion be comprised of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: A motorised battalion mostly consists of infantry units on motor vehicles, so it's an infantry battalion -- a motorised infantry battalion. As for weaponry, it has all infantry weapons; it has 82-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, and anti-aircraft guns of 40 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: According to the rules and regulations of the Yugoslav People's Army, what would have been the required response if, given this presence, there was an incursion of an armed non-regular force of men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: According to the regulations and the tasks of the JNA, my commander, according to all the rules and regulations then in force, should have issued an order that this group should be arrested and placed under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the latter part of the first week in April 1992. Did you see on the television a video clip of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic's visit to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: After the events in Bijeljina, the massacre that was carried out, Biljana Plavsic, a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, arrived there, as well as Fikret Abdic, a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Colonel General Prasovic arrived, the chief of staff of the 2nd Military District. I saw Biljana Plavsic embracing and kissing the man who had carried out the massacre in Bijeljina. I saw Colonel General Prasovic practically reporting to Arkan and praising him for having completed his task well instead of doing what I have just mentioned, arresting the entire group.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The 2nd Military District, over what area did that military district have responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The 2nd Military District was established after the dissolution of the 5th Military District, which was the Zagreb district. It had its seat in Sarajevo, and Colonel General Milutin Kukanjac was at its head. The Chief of Staff was General Prasovic, and its area of responsibility was the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, parts of the Knin Krajina, parts of Slavonia and Baranja, and practically the territory as far as the Danube and the Drina Rivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now ask you to look at a video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I might say to the Chamber, the portion of the video that I'd like to witness to comment on goes by very quickly. So I've actually made two stills of the video, and I would like to show the stills first so that when the video does play, everyone in the court will be attuned to the moment in time that I will ask the witness to speak about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to look at the monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask the usher to set it up for Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the photograph before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: On this photograph, I recognise the chief of the 2nd Military District, General Prasovic, with his hand raised in salute, reporting to Arkan. On this picture, he is greeting Arkan after reporting to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are both these photographs from a video of this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: These photographs were shown on the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the clip be played, and I will ask for your comments afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would note that this is a clip from Serbian television, and this is Prosecution Exhibit 425, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Here we can see again the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Military District in the centre, Lieutenant General Prasovic. To his right is Fikret Abdic, and to his left is Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 425, tab 2. I'd ask that the original B/C/S version be handed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to take a look at this document, in particular the person who authored the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: This is a document that was drawn up every day, and by 2000 hours it had to be sent to the superior command. This was a daily operative report sent by the command to its superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like you to read the first -- the first sentence following the number 2. If you could just read that aloud for us, the first sentence of number 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: "The combat readiness of corps units ensures fulfilment of the task. All units are at the highest level of combat readiness, especially the forces of Operative Group 1 and those in the Bijeljina Garrison."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please stop. I just want to ask you to comment on that one sentence. Does that sentence indicate that the JNA in the Bijeljina Garrison was at full capacity or full combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: According to this report by the commander dispatching this, the units in the Bijeljina area are fully manned, fully equipped with materiel and equipment, and they are in a state of full combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based on your experience, would the Bijeljina Garrison at this state of readiness been equipped and able to have dealt with the incursion of Arkan and his men into the Bijeljina area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The units that are in Bijeljina, not to mention those in the immediate vicinity of Bijeljina near Janja where there was a large number of tanks, could very easily have dealt with this special purpose unit brought by Arkan which carried out an aggression and which was armed neither with tanks nor with APCs. They had mainly light weapons and anti-aircraft guns with single-barrel and three-barrel guns. So there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would have been no problem for the JNA units, those in the barracks, to have dealt with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you now to read the first sentence following the number 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: "The situation in the territory is extremely complex. The town of Bijeljina is controlled by the SDS and Arkan's men, who do not even allow our anti-tank unit to reach certain positions in the town."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask for your comment on that sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I have information from a lieutenant colonel who was a commanding officer that there were two tanks in Bijeljina, and with one tank and one platoon of soldiers he had tried to go out of the barracks and he had been slapped by Arkan. His superior command ordered him to return to barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to two other sentences in the document, the next one being the first sentence following the number 8, "Conclusion."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: "The security and political situation in the corps' zone of responsibility is very complex and in certain areas it's even critical (Bosanski Brod and Bijeljina). There is a real danger that the situation might considerably deteriorate in the municipalities of Zvornik, Tuzla, Zivinice and Brcko, including the threat of inter-ethnic conflicts with incalculable consequences."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As a matter of ordinary course of operations for the JNA, would the chief of staff have been made aware of this commander's assessment of the situation in these municipalities mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The chief of staff had to be completely aware of the situation because he was the one planning and conducting combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the last sentence I would ask you to read is the last sentence of the document, just above the commander's name and signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the impression that there is something unclear here. I understood Mr. Groome to be asking whether the chief of the general staff of the JNA had to be aware of this, and the witness was speaking of the chief of staff of a lower-level unit. To clear up this misunderstanding, I ask for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you can clarify it, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was asking you about the chief of the general staff. Can you please comment on whether he would have been made aware of the situation under the ordinary course of operations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In principle, according to all the military rules and regulations then in force in the JNA, the chief of staff was the highest-ranking officer in charge of a staff and he was responsible for the planning and execution of all military operations, and from the highest to the lowest level, the chief of staff would have to be completely informed of the whole situation on the ground and the situation in the units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now could I ask you to read the last sentence of the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: "The measures of heightened combat readiness in commands and units have been taken to ensure adequate protection of people and lives, weapons and equipment --" "The measures taken of heightened combat readiness in commands and units ensure adequate protection of people and lives, weapons and equipment in all the units of the corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would this line -- would this particular sentence indicate that it was this commander's view that he was in a position to adequately protect the people and lives of the people within his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In my personal opinion, when it says here "adequate protection of people and lives," that the commander who sent this combat report was referring to his men and his units, that he was not referring to the population in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask now that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 425, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is a telegram. I want to draw your attention to a handwritten note on the telegram. Do you recognise the handwriting of that handwritten note?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, I know the handwriting very well. I have seen it many times. I also know the signature; I recognise it. The handwriting belongs to Lieutenant General Milutin Kukanjac, the commander of the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to read a portion of this telegram. I'm going to ask you to read the first line, and I will, if you don't mind, interrupt you about halfway through it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: "I hereby inform you that in Mali Zvornik the chief negotiator with the representatives of the Zvornik Municipal Assembly and the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik was Arkan. The negotiations were also attended by Captain Dragan Obrenovic as well as Alija and Abdulah and Jovo Mijatovic. Arkan was the chief negotiator on behalf of the other side, and two representatives were previously beaten up. Zvornik needs to lay down its arms, and the Crisis Staff of the Zvornik Municipal Assembly should make a decision on the ultimatum by 1600 hours. I do not think that the ultimatum will be accepted and I believe that this will lead to an unprecedented massacre of the unprotected and innocent population and to horrible environmental consequences as a result of suicidal action by the probably desperate --" it probably means desperate -- "population. I send you this dispatch as a cry to heaven and an appeal to you to in line with the most illustrious traditions of the JNA and the highest moral norms of our people to protect the --" it says here "respectable population" -- "from a disaster --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it says -- it doesn't say "respectable," it says "endangered," the endangered population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, one letter is missing. All right. All right. "Endangered." "... the endangered population from a catastrophe such as they have never before experienced, probably, in their history." Experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is the author of this cable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: This telegram was written by Izet Mehinagic. He was the director of the public company for the construction of the Tuzla-Zvornik railway and a great friend of General Milutin Kukanjac. I know that they socialised while the gentleman was in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the resources of the JNA that were in the area of Zvornik and Mali Zvornik that would have been in a position to have interceded when Arkan arrived in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I said that when the 4th Armoured Brigade arrived from Jastrebarsko one battalion of that brigade was deployed in Zvornik, and the brigade on its own could have challenged Arkan. This battalion of the armoured brigade on its own could have dealt with him effectively. However, in the vicinity of Zvornik, there were far more significant units, some 30 or 40 kilometres away. These were motorised units, they were well armed, and they could have arrived in Zvornik very quickly. And had such an order been issued, they could have responded and prevented the massacre that was carried out in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could read the handwriting portion also.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That was my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please read the handwritten note of General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: "To Jankovic to take all measures to protect citizens in Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: First it says, "Inform General Jankovic." That's precisely what it says. "Inform General Jankovic to take all measures to protect citizens in Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your view, were all measures taken to protect the citizens of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: We know what the result was of the activities of Arkan and the other units attacking Zvornik. Practically not a single unit of the JNA was activated to prevent what Arkan did in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes. We will allow time for discussion of the procedural matters concerning the witnesses under Rule 92 bis at half past 1.00. We'll continue with cross-examination after the 20-minutes' adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies. I neglected to ask a couple of questions regarding cultural property, which this witness has personal knowledge. May I reopen my examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever present or do you have any personal knowledge regarding the destruction of mosques and other cultural property?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of which I was in command, I was present and I did see quite a number of religious and cultural buildings being blown up or hit by artillery during the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to just list the municipalities where you have this knowledge of cultural property and religious property being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In the municipality of Gradacac, all the mosques were destroyed, mostly with artillery. In the municipality of Brcko, all the mosques have been destroyed, mostly by being blown up. In Bijeljina municipality, all five mosques were destroyed by planting explosives and blowing them up. In the municipality of Kladanj, the minaret of the mosque was directly hit and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based upon your own personal knowledge, are you aware or were there any indications to you that with respect to the artillery used to damage this religious property, that it was used in such a way that indicated to you that it was not collateral damage but intended damage to the property?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Religious property was destroyed not in the course of combat operations but by being directly targeted. That is, the minaret was targeted and they would be cut in half. In a locality called Rahic, the mosque was destroyed by a direct hit with a plane bomb. I was nearby when it was destroyed. So that these religious buildings were not destroyed in the course of combat operations but by intentional destruction of religious buildings so that no trace of them would remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1493, you started your testimony this morning by explaining how plans were made. And as I have noted down here, the words you used were "the danger of a possible internal enemy, that is, extremists of the HDZ"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I said that the plan was headed "Engagement of units of which I was in command in the event of the introduction of a state of emergency," and in the text of the order mention was made as a potential internal enemy extremist sections of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is what I wish to establish. You received that assignment to prepare the plan in March 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And were you aware of the events in Croatia in 1990 and up until March 1991 when you were assigned to compile that plan? What was going on? What was happening to the Serbs in Croatia up until that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I do know what was happening in those areas in Croatia. I know of the Balvan or log revolution in the Knin Krajina, I am aware of the events at Plitvice lakes where policemen were killed, and some other such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in precisely that period of time, that is, in 1990 up until March 1991, persecution in the broader sense of Serbs in Croatia were -- was underway? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: As a good portion of Croatia was in the area of responsibility of the unit of which I was a member and I went to areas quite a number of times that were mostly inhabited by Serbs, I do not know of a single example of Serbs being persecuted in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of the unit of which you were a member, includes the parts of Croatia known as Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem, Pozega, so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I am referring precisely to those areas, and I do not know that up until 1991 there was a single case of an organised persecution of the civilian population in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that there were a series of silent liquidations of individual Serbs in those areas? Do you recall the activities of groups headed by Tomislav Mercep in Eastern Slavonia? Do you still remember the secret arming of the HDZ? Do you remember the dismissals, especially from the police, the state administration and public services of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with these one at a time. So the first question was -- just a moment. It's -- I know you say it's cumulative, but the witness can't answer a list of questions. He can only answer one question at a time. Now, the first question is: Do you know about the liquidation of individual Serbs? Was there any, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the knowledge I have, the authorities in power at the time in the Republic of Croatia did not in an organised manner carry out silent individual liquidations. If there were any such liquidations, there may have been settling of accounts between debtors or political opponents. But as I was saying, in the area of responsibility in which I was working and living, there is -- it is quite certain that there were no organised liquidations of Serbs by non-Serbs. I am saying this up until May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What about these other tendencies that I mentioned? Do you remember that Serbs were expelled from the constitution as a constituent nation? Do you remember the decision on the secession of Croatia? Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. Before we get on to the political matters, you were asked about the activities of Tomislav Mercep. Do you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the activities of the mentioned group, I know nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or it's suggested the -- there was a secret arming of the HDZ. Do you know anything about that, if there was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding secret arming, that is common knowledge that there were -- that it did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you in the JNA have then and up until then, when you were assigned this task of preparing the plan, that there was a resurrection of the Ustasha movement in Croatia and that forcible secession from Yugoslavia was about to take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Up until our work on that plan, that is, until 1991, I was not aware that in the area where I was a single unit was formed or any organised Ustasha groupings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you knew nothing about secession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you know anything about large-scale dismissals of Serb members of the police and public services?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In the police of the Republic of Croatia, after 1991 I did come across in Zagreb and in Slavonski Brod and in Osijek policemen of Serb ethnicity. Probably there were dismissals of those who did not abide by the laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. A moment ago you said that you did know about secession; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you in the army consider it to be the duty of the JNA to protect the integrity of the country? Is that one of its priority duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I said that the Yugoslav People's Army, its first and foremost task was to protect the unity and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, was it not logical for the army to prepare a plan to be able to carry out that task, to protect the integrity of the country, which unfortunately didn't succeed but at least to try to protect it? Why is that unusual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: According to my modest knowledge as a high-ranking officer of the JNA, it is my conviction that the top-level military leadership came under the very powerful influence of the political leadership and it did not undertake the measures which the general staff, headed by the federal secretary, should have undertaken because it succumbed to influence and the orders of the political leadership that was at the time at the head of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that then, that is, in March 1991 and before March 1991 and even after March 1991, this top-level military leadership was by ethnicity least of all Serbian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The chief of the general staff in those days was Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A Serb from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: A Serb from Gacko and Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The federal secretary was Veljko Kadijevic, from Imotsko, who was from a mixed Serb-Croat marriage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: He was a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a Yugoslav. And who was the commander of your army district?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: For a short period, Spirkovksi was the commander of the 1st Military District and he was replaced shortly after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was commander of the 5th one in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: At first it was a Croat and he was replaced shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in 1991 he wasn't the commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: In 1991, Spegelj was no longer the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was commander only in 1990, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on to the next matter that you addressed at the very beginning of your examination-in-chief. On the 2nd of May, you were given an order and went to Vinkovci with a joint detachment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was a joint detachment consisting of five platoons, as you said, and the strength was about 120 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the assignment you were given was to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts in the area to which you were dispatched; is that right? That is, the broader area around Vinkovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, from Vinkovci towards Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened in Borovo Selo immediately prior to that? Are you aware of the incursion of the police that opened fire on the citizens of Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this was their reaction; the sending of two JNA detachments came after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were you aware that having been sent there for that particular reason, what was the reason for the police to open fire on peasants in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Because fire was opened at the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So the police came to Borovo Selo for it to be fired upon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The police was already in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't you know that the police came to Borovo Selo in two buses and several other vehicles, came out of those vehicles and opened fire quite unreasonably on the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. But the police had come to intervene after a conflict had broken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was the conflict between in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point, Mr. Milosevic. This witness has no direct evidence of these events in Borovo Selo. There's no point really arguing with him about it. Let's move on to something he does know about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. May, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the night between the 2nd and 3rd of May you arrived in Vinkovci, and then in the morning you started off to Mirkovci and you then described the incidents in the area between Mirkovci and Jankovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that in front of Mirkovci you came across a roadblock manned by a total of three men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any other barricades in Mirkovci on the way out towards Jankovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Upon leaving the village of Mirkovci, there were no barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from those three men and their commander who they called to talk to you, did you see any other men with arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: According to the report of my military police patrol, they -- from a house that was burning, they saw four armed men dressed in the same uniforms as those at the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you established as the head of that unit, you had three men at the roadblock and their commander, and you also established that there were another four men that were seen in Jankovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I saw that, but from the president of the local community of Mirkovci, at a meeting with them, I was told that a unit had come to Mirkovci, a large unit, which had spread out in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I did not see the unit. As I say, I only saw the three men at the roadblock -- or rather, four, and I was informed by the patrol that there were another four who had set fire to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you had a detachment 120 strong, a regular JNA unit. You say that you saw men in some sort of Chetnik uniforms. And we have now established that you saw three of them, or rather, four of them -- plus four, a total of seven. So tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Eight. I'm sorry, eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine, eight. Why did you not -- considering them to have provoked the conflict -- was that your conclusion, that they had provoked the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: My conclusion when I came across the roadblock was not such that those men at the barricades had caused anything. People were lying down next to the machine-guns and they had bandoliers on them and the machine-guns were pointing towards Vinkovci, that is, the direction from which my detachment was coming, and they were not opening fire. But obviously those other men were firing where I had sent the police patrol, and they set the house on fire, so it was them who had provoked the clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as far as I was able to see, they were members of one and the same unit, weren't they, they were one and the same group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these three at the roadblock, and the four you saw burning a house in Jankovci, they were surely members of the same group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: They were not the same group because these ones remained at the roadblock, and the four of them who were burning the house, they fled -- or rather, withdrew towards Mirkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were already between Mirkovci and Jankovci, so you were in a sense in control of Mirkovci by then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I had passed through Mirkovci. I've explained that. And the head of the column reached the village of Jankovci. When I saw the house on fire and I heard the shooting, I explained that I stopped the column and I ordered the detachment to deploy in combat formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as you were a high-ranking officer then and later, was it clear to you that this was a paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The one at the barricade and the other four you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, both.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: It was clear to me that this was not a unit belonging to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it could have only been a paramilitary unit or a group of criminals or something like that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, precisely what is known as a paramilitary formation. But I think it was a well-organised unit since this commander who came out to the roadblock and said that he would let me through when he is given permission from his commander in Sremska Mitrovica, so it seems -- it appeared that the control and command system in the unit was well established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not talk about the control and command in a unit of eight men. But tell me, since you were sent there to re-establish order, why didn't you disarm and arrest those men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I didn't do that because I would have probably provoked a conflict between my detachment and that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But wasn't that your job to do that, to -- since you yourself say that you were given the assignment to restore order, isn't it the job of an armed group of soldiers of the JNA who have the assignment to restore order to disarm such a unit and arrest those men? Why were you going there otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I went there in order to prevent an inter-ethnic conflict between two villages of different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was it clear from what you say that those people were participating in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you stop them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Because that was not my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your task did not include the use of your unit but only an inspection of the situation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: And preventing a conflict between the inhabitants of Mirkovci and Jankovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who was it who was having a fight among the inhabitants of Mirkovci and Jankovci? Was it a fight between Serbs, among themselves, or was it Croatian forces and Serbian forces that were in conflict there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: When I arrived, there was no conflict of local people from Mirkovci and Jankovci. I explained that a house was on fire. In the basement of that house -- or rather, on the ground floor there was an inn and the local Serbs whose houses were right next to that inn - there were four Serb houses - they explained to me that this group had arrived, driven out all the people who happened to be in the pub, driven out the owner of the house, that they had then set the house on fire, and that they were causing disruption and disorder. So the local people asked to be protected from that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Serbs living there asked you to protect -- asked you to protect them from them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But still you didn't arrest them. You have just said you didn't want to arrest them in order not to cause a conflict between the two villages. You were informed that these were not local people, that this was a group that had arrived from elsewhere, and yet you did not disarm and arrest them, even though they had come from elsewhere. And then it was clear that this would not have caused a conflict between the two villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Well, the tactics were to introduce a paramilitary unit to cause disruption, to cause a conflict, and then to send in larger units, and that was a scenario. Very soon after I left, the unit -- there was an attack from Mirkovci to Jankovci and Jankovci was practically occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was that not an even stronger reason for you to intervene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I did introduce order there. The shooting stopped while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Evidently we cannot agree on this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: It's precisely because I introduced order that I was replaced and another commander was brought in. After a few days of his arrival, a conflict broke out where the detachment I had arrived in participated in the conflict and practically blockaded the village of Jankovci and then made it possible for that situation to be forced out, for that population to be expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the detachment you brought there later acted against the civilian population in Jankovci.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, together with the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this seems quite incredible to me. But you sent a written report about what had happened and what you had seen on the ground; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, I sent a regular combat report to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: No, I don't. I wasn't allowed to keep it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't keep a copy of the report you were sending? It was your report you were sending? You don't have your own report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: We never had the right to keep copies of our reports because this was of a strictly confidential nature and it was sent only to the command that had given us our orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you sent this report, and on the basis of this report, the answer you received was that you should stay there and make sure that the situation was calm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the person who came to replace you, was he of a lower rank than you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: He was of the same rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of the same rank? And how do you explain the reason for this switch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I didn't have to explain this to anyone. I received an order from my superior commander that I should hand over my duty and return to my home unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that your superior officer, when you got back and explained that you had seen some kind of Chetniks, as you say - I've written down the word you used here - that he said to you that this was impossible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: He didn't say it was impossible. He said, "You have seen tomcats."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't this confirm to you that there would have been no conflict had you carried out your task, arrested those people, and performed the task that you were supposed to perform there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: There probably would have been a conflict because in that village there were more members of that unit and there would have been an armed conflict, and I was not ready for this, nor was this my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were not prepared to perform your role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I performed my role very well, and this was recognised by the local inhabitants of the village of Jankovci, the four families of Serb ethnicity who, on the 6th or 7th of May, asked my superior command to send me back to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened? Who was it who decided that you should not be sent back or that the situation should not be cleared up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: My superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you feel that you performed your task, although you engaged in no operations and that's why you were sent there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I think that my first wartime assignment I carried out with honour and I am proud of this. I have been praised for this by the villagers of Jankovci who sent a letter to my superior command asking me to be sent back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the next event you spoke of. You spoke of the mobilisation of the brigade in Bijeljina, and you said that one of the generals - you said he was a general - gave an unusual address and that he did not behave as members of the JNA were supposed to. What was the name of this general?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The general's name was Rajko Lapcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he the commander of that brigade, or what was he? What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: He was the chief of staff of a high unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The chief of staff of a high-level unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your assessment and according to what you say, his speech ran completely counter to the behaviour expected of a high-ranking JNA officer; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I made my statement in which I said that this was the first time in my long military career that I heard this kind of greeting and this kind of moral political preparation of soldiers for the execution of their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you heard for the first time was in your opinion against all the rules of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were a high-ranking officer, did you inform your superior command of this and did you initiate what it was your duty to do, an initiative to take measures against such behaviour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I told you that at that time I was no longer holding a high-level post because in September 1991 I was removed from my important post and assigned to an insignificant post in the Department for Mobilisation. Secondly, I can confirm that General Kukanjac was the corps commander in Macedonia, and the same evening, since I knew him well - we'd worked together for a long time - at around midnight I rang him up and informed him of what had happened because previously he had been this man's commander. And I can say this: The gentleman who made the speech was very quickly replaced and moved to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, explain how this was possible. As far as I could understand, you phoned General Kukanjac in Macedonia to inform him of this and you did not go to the authority that was in charge and which was certainly accessible to you to inform them of this and to ask that appropriate measures be taken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: There were higher-ranking officers in that team who should have informed the commander of what had happened, so it was not my duty nor did I have the right to report to my commander about this. And I rang up Kukanjac precisely because we had worked together for a long time, because I knew him well, and because for many years Kukanjac had been in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I informed him out of friendship and not out of my command duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you had no duty to inform anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying, because I was one of the lowest-ranking officers of the 20 of us taking part there. My post was one of the lowest in that team, and the -- others should have reported to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if the one whose duty it is doesn't do it, the others don't have to do this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: It is not their duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's clarify one more point: You explained the use of the Territorial Defence; is that correct? You spoke of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I explained the chain of command in the Territorial Defence in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the republican staff of the Territorial Defence was in charge of the TO in every republic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the republican Territorial Defence staff of any republic was exclusively subordinate to the general staff of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: The republican TO staff was the republican staff, and it was subordinate to the republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying the opposite. Have you read the law? I tendered this into evidence here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: When the weapons were taken from the Territorial Defence and when all the preparations were being made for what would take place, not only were the weapons taken from the Territorial Defence but the law was changed and the republican staffs were placed under the chain of command of the general staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the republican staffs were under the command of the general staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Well, just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's what matters. It was the JNA. Did the general staff order that weapons be taken from the TO and that it was not done only in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: This order came from the top control and command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that weapons were taken, regardless of ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In the area where I was, regardless of ethnicity, all the weapons were placed under the control of my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In JNA depots, under the guard of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me now: You say in February and March some kind of distribution of weapons to municipal staffs of the Territorial Defence began in areas where there were Serbs. That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I didn't say "some kind of distribution," I said "organised removal of weapons of the Territorial Defence of the municipal staffs," and I listed Sekovic, Vlasenica, Lopare. I -- anyway, in places where the majority population was Serb. It is not "some kind," but it was organised taking of weapons and equipment. Columns were formed, the weapons were transported, and there was a place called MZ where the weapons were distributed. I was personally present at the distribution of such weapons in the village of Sekovici, on the playing field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. This morning you testified to seeing weapons being driven off, that you saw this personally. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, could you have known where the weapons were being taken? You were at the point from which the weapons were being taken away, so how do you know where they were taken? Were they taken to some safer depots, or were they distributed? You couldn't have been in both places at once.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I was also present at places where weapons were distributed. I repeat: In the village of Sekovici, I was present when weapons were distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just look in your statement. I'm following the same order as in this morning's examination-in-chief. Just a moment, please. I have noted it down here. You say that a referendum was held in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You mentioned it this morning, didn't you? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: Yes. It is well known that there was a referendum on the 1st of March. That is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you said this morning that it was normal, because, you see, Croatian Slovenia was seceding, so it was only normal for Bosnia and Herzegovina to do the same. However, I hope you have the statement in front of you. On page 3, in paragraph 8 of your statement, you say that you, both Serb and non-Serb officers, considered the referendum for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina held in March 1992 to be a betrayal of SFRY.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: That is not my statement. I don't have the statement in front of me, but that is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll show it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's no need for us to argue over that. Please find page 3, paragraph 8 and read it, please. Read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be sure that we're talking about the same document, there are actually two statements, one dated the 20th of April, 2002 and one dated the 22nd of May, 2002. Which statement is Mr. Milosevic referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us that, please. Wait. Let's just make sure we've got the right statement. Which statement are you referring to? What's the date, please, on the front?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find it just now, but I think he has it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may be of assistance, Your Honours. I think it is the statement of the 20th of April, 2002. And it is quite correct what has just been quoted. It is on page 3, second paragraph from the bottom. Would you be kind enough to read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me say first of all that I never made such a statement, as I was one of the first, maybe the first, to go to the ballot box where a vote was being cast for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Whether it is a slip, an error in the translation...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read out that very brief paragraph of two lines, please, from your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I can't read it, when that is not my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just -- let somebody else read it out, then. Perhaps, Mr. Tapuskovic, you read it so we can hear what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is one sentence, and it reads as follows: "We (Serbian and not Serbian officers of JNA) considered the referendum for the independence of BH which was held in March 1992 to be a betrayal of SFRY." That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've heard what the explanation of the witness is. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, two more minutes and then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard that he said it wasn't his statement, but we've also heard that I quoted correctly from what I have received as his statement, so I hope that that is not at issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also, tell me, Mr. 1493, do you remember that all of us in Yugoslavia, in SFRY, considered Bosnia and Herzegovina to be Yugoslavia in miniature, especially and particularly because it was inhabited by three ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: While there was Yugoslavia, such as it was, all of us in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Yugoslavia were proud of that Yugoslavia. However, after the death of Comrade Tito, after all kinds of changes, this gradually disappeared and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please: For you, without entering into the ground of morality but talking about political, economic material things, was it logical for such a Bosnia and Herzegovina, a Yugoslavia in miniature, composed of three different nations, to separate from Yugoslavia? Was that logical to you? You said you were the first to vote for that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1493
utterances.text: I think that at that polling station I was the first to vote. It was quite logical after the sequence of events that took place and the betrayal by the top political and military leadership. Slovenia was being written off as a state, or rather, a republic, and independence was being granted to it. Croatia -- none of the proposals by members of the Presidencies of the republics in those days for Yugoslavia to remain within its borders, for all peoples to lead normal lives, for it to be organised as a confederation, but exclusivity mostly on the part of the Serbian leadership insisted on Yugoslavia remaining the way they had wanted it to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must continue this tomorrow. We have to go on to deal with procedural matters. Mr. Milosevic, you can have an hour and a quarter tomorrow morning to conclude your cross-examination of this witness. It will be yet again longer than the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please take into consideration the possibility of giving me a little more time than one hour, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see how -- we'll see how we get on tomorrow. Witness B-1493, that concludes your evidence for today. We have to deal with some other matters. Would you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning to conclude your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. McKeon deals with the 92 bis, can I remind the Court, but more particularly the accused, through Your Honours, that tomorrow's witness is to be the financial expert, Mr. Torkildsen, and to alert the accused to the fact that I will probably be very brief in examination-in-chief, not of course in order to restrict the accused to the same amount of limited time that I will take but because that is the appropriate way to deal with expert witnesses wherever that can properly be done. It shall take some time, but not very much time with him, I hope, in chief, and it will then be for the accused to cross-examine him. The only other general administrative matter I'd make is this: If the Chamber is going to say anything about the examination-in-chief by the means of 92 bis or otherwise, although we have pretty well fixed in our order of witnesses and number of witnesses for the period until the Easter break, we are in a position to change and to increase the rate of witnesses for after the Easter break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have that in mind. Now let us turn to these 92 bis witnesses. The list which I have, 1154, 1168, 1187, 1230, 1232, 1234, and Mr. McKeon has added 1197 and 1210. We'll try and get through as many as we can. Dealing first with 1154, this is a doctor, my note has it, from Beli Manastir in Baranja, who performed a series of autopsies. We've admitted such evidence without cross-examination. In this case, Mr. Kay, any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't have any additional observation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Then moving to the next one, 68. This is another witness from Baranja who deals with the arrest of her husband and his mistreatment and subsequent murder and her efforts to find him. Yes. Anything about that one, Mr. McKeon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, I would note that this particular witness has already been described by witness -- I'm sorry, the victim has been described by Witness C-25, so this would be cumulative to that testimony which is already before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps so we can let -- give Mr. Kay a minute or two. 1187 is a very similar witness. Her son was arrested from the same area by, I think, people she describes as two Serbs, although I may be wrong about that. And he hadn't been seen since. Again, anything as to that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Just to -- to add, Your Honour, the Court has already allowed us to put in under 92 bis the testimony of Witness C-1052, which is very similar to this witness except that it involves -- C-1052 involves the first Dalj massacre and this witness essentially provides similar testimony as to the second Dalj massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And is -- is that one, that second witness, required to attend for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if you could deal with those two, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. 11 -- C-1168, which is tab 41, it's cumulative over the white minivan issue, which the Trial Chamber may be aware of by -- from C-25. There's an issue from the -- a JNA captain, which is a matter of hearsay, reporting about the husband.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where -- where would we -- can you tell us where that one is? Oh, yes. "My husband had to report twice a day. He told me most of the time he reported to a JNA captain." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the issue on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's one sentence. If that sentence was taken out, which as you rightly point out it's hearsay anyway, there's no reason why it shouldn't be admitted without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The issue of the white minivan is quite an important issue in the case. It features within the indictment as to the taking away of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In looking at 1187, I couldn't find any apparent link to C-25 when I was going through the statement and the evidence after a number of -- of careful checks. I may be wrong about it and have missed something of -- of relevance, but I couldn't actually see any link there to that particular witness. I don't know if the Prosecution is able to help the Trial Chamber in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may be something that we'll have to look at. Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to point out that C-25 testified about the arrest of -- of people in the Baranja area. This was a particular victim who was transported as -- as that witness testified about, to Dalj, where other evidence would show that he was subsequently murdered, and that's the connection with C-25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next three we're moving to a different area. I'm sorry, were you going to -- did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I didn't want to add anything to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next three are dealing with I think it's the Saborsko area. I could be wrong. But Poljanac and Saborsko. One deals with -- C-1230, I should say, the first one, deals with an attack on Poljanac, but he identifies the Nis special unit of the JNA. And I suppose, Mr. Kay, you would say that's rather a crucial issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the running objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
